summary.text: For \(k\ge 60\), set \(n=2k+1\); the two primes associated with any nonzero matrix entry sum to \(2n=4k+2\), so the absence of a Goldbach decomposition would make the entire matrix zero and contradict the assumed nonzero determinant. The remaining cases \(1\le k<60\) are handled by explicit prime decompositions.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\det M_n,
\]
where the rows and columns of the \(n\times n\) matrix \(M_n\) are indexed by \(i,j\in\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}\), and
\[
(M_n)_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
The subtractions here may be regarded as natural-number subtractions. They do not truncate in this range: since \(j\le n-1<n\le n+i\), we have \(n+i\ge j\), and similarly \(n+j\ge i\).

Assume the stated nonvanishing conjecture:
\[
\text{for every odd }n>120,\qquad a(n)\ne0.
\tag{1}
\]
We prove that for every positive integer \(k\), the integer \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

First dispose of the finite range \(1\le k<60\). The following table gives the required prime decomposition in every case:
\[
\begin{array}{c|r@{\;=\;}r@{+}l||c|r@{\;=\;}r@{+}l}
k&4k+2&p&q&k&4k+2&p&q\\ \hline
1&6&3&3&31&126&13&113\\
2&10&3&7&32&130&3&127\\
3&14&3&11&33&134&3&131\\
4&18&5&13&34&138&7&131\\
5&22&3&19&35&142&3&139\\
6&26&3&23&36&146&7&139\\
7&30&7&23&37&150&11&139\\
8&34&3&31&38&154&3&151\\
9&38&7&31&39&158&7&151\\
10&42&5&37&40&162&5&157\\
11&46&3&43&41&166&3&163\\
12&50&3&47&42&170&3&167\\
13&54&7&47&43&174&7&167\\
14&58&5&53&44&178&5&173\\
15&62&3&59&45&182&3&179\\
16&66&5&61&46&186&5&181\\
17&70&3&67&47&190&11&179\\
18&74&3&71&48&194&3&191\\
19&78&5&73&49&198&5&193\\
20&82&3&79&50&202&3&199\\
21&86&3&83&51&206&7&199\\
22&90&7&83&52&210&11&199\\
23&94&5&89&53&214&3&211\\
24&98&19&79&54&218&7&211\\
25&102&5&97&55&222&11&211\\
26&106&3&103&56&226&3&223\\
27&110&3&107&57&230&3&227\\
28&114&5&109&58&234&5&229\\
29&118&5&113&59&238&5&233\\
30&122&13&109&&&&
\end{array}
\]
Every number appearing in either of the last two columns of a decomposition is prime. This is a direct finite check: the largest is \(233\), so for each number it is enough to test divisibility by primes no larger than \(\sqrt{233}<16\), namely \(2,3,5,7,11,13\) (with the number itself omitted when appropriate). The displayed additions also directly give \(p+q=4k+2\). Thus the claim holds for all \(1\le k<60\).

It remains to treat \(k\ge60\). Set
\[
n=2k+1.
\]
Then \(n\) is odd, and
\[
n=2k+1\ge121>120.
\]
Consequently, hypothesis (1) says
\[
\det M_n=a(n)\ne0.
\tag{2}
\]

We claim that some entry of \(M_n\) must equal \(1\). Indeed, suppose to the contrary that \(4k+2\) had no representation as a sum of two primes. Consider arbitrary row and column indices
\[
0\le i,j<n.
\]
Put
\[
p=n+i-j,\qquad q=n+j-i.
\]
As noted above, these natural-number subtractions are exact: \(j\le n-1<n\le n+i\) and \(i\le n-1<n\le n+j\). Therefore ordinary cancellation is valid, and
\[
p+q=(n+i-j)+(n+j-i)=2n=2(2k+1)=4k+2.
\tag{3}
\]
If both \(p\) and \(q\) were prime, equation (3) would be precisely a representation of \(4k+2\) as a sum of two primes, contrary to the supposition. Thus for every pair \((i,j)\), at least one of \(p,q\) is not prime. By the definition of \(M_n\), every entry \((M_n)_{ij}\) is consequently zero. Hence \(M_n\) is the zero matrix.

Since \(n\ge121\), this matrix has positive size. The determinant of a positive-size zero matrix is zero: in the permutation expansion of the determinant, every term is a product of matrix entries and hence contains only zero factors. It follows that
\[
a(n)=\det M_n=0,
\]
contradicting (2). The supposition was therefore false. Hence there exist primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
4k+2=p+q.
\]

Combining this argument for \(k\ge60\) with the explicit finite table for \(1\le k<60\), we conclude that every integer of the form \(4k+2\) with \(k>0\) is the sum of two primes.
